title: Physical cast layouts: UINT2, FP4, dual FP8 and HiFloat8 both directions
surface: Ten kernel(mode="vec") cast entries: BF16 to packed UINT2 carriers and back with an explicit padding row, BF16 to FP4 E1M2 nibble pairs, one source row cast to float8_e5m2 and float8_e4m3fn in a single launch, and HiFloat8 carriers decoded to FP32/FP16 and encoded from them under two rounding policies
study_for: Every reference is built from the format's bit layout -- a code table, shifts and masks -- and calls no library codec. That is what makes agreement evidence about the cast instruction instead of a comparison of the library with itself, and it is why the boundary cases can be trusted.

Four cases are exhaustive rather than sampled: `fp4_all_finite_bf16` enumerates all 65024 finite BF16 words, and the two `*_all_bits` cases enumerate all 65536 half-precision words. At these widths the whole input space fits in a run, so a rounding boundary cannot be missed by construction -- and a sampled case would never establish the same thing.

The two HiFloat8 rounding policies, `ta` and `hybrid`, appear as separate entries over the same source words. Their pair is the subject: the codes agree everywhere except where the policies differ, so running one alone tells you nothing about which one you have.

`uint2_unpack` takes its padding as an explicit argument, and three cases hand it 0, 0xA5 and random bytes. 0xA5 is chosen because all four of its 2-bit fields are non-zero, so padding that leaked into a result is unmistakable. main.py compares the three runs' outputs to each other -- no single case can state that the padding does not matter.

`fp8_dual` writes E5M2 and E4M3 from one launch, so both lattices see exactly the same source values. `fp8_boundaries` gives it every representable value of both lattices, every midpoint, the neighbour on each side of each, and the infinities and NaN -- which is where a tie that rounds the wrong way, or a saturation where an overflow belongs, becomes visible.

The comparison is byte equality with exactly one exemption: two NaNs agree whatever their payloads hold, because the payload of a NaN result is not specified by these formats. Nothing else is loosened -- and since HiFloat8 has a single zero code, the sign of zero never arises here, while anywhere else a flipped zero sign would be a different byte and a failure.
do_not_copy_when: You are treating a NaN payload as defined. It is not, which is the one place this example's comparison is not a byte comparison. If your kernel depends on a particular NaN payload, that dependency is outside anything established here.
Your UINT2 input is not exactly 0, 1, 2 or 3 in BF16. The packing entry accepts only those; what it does with a non-integral or out-of-range value is not covered.
Your FP4 input is not finite. The preserved domain is finite BF16, and infinities and NaNs through the FP4 packing are not part of this example.

You are assuming a padding row cannot affect an unpacked result. This example checks that it does not, across three different padding rows -- checking is the point, and a single padding value would not have made the statement.

You expect one rounding policy to stand for the other. `ta` and `hybrid` are separate entries because they differ; picking one and assuming the other matches is the mistake the pair exists to prevent.
